We introduce and investigate the global permutation properties of two specific types of polynomials within the space $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}} \rightarrow \mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Specifically, the first family of polynomials has a degree of 3 in their leading term and coefficients from $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ for the second degree term. The global permutation properties of these polynomials vary across different types of prime powers. Conversely, the third family of polynomials exhibits a consistent and non-trivial permutation property across all prime powers. Moreover, by combining these polynomials with elements from the group $PGL_{2}(\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}})$, we generate an extensive variety of permutation polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$.

This research introduces a novel deep belief network architecture, which leverages Hidden Markov Models and Undirected Probabilistic Graphical Models, to automatically categorize full-body images of intestinal parasites based on their shape and structure. The Undirected Probabilistic Graphical Model component encodes the spatial relationships of the parasite's shape, while the deep belief network encodes its structural characteristics, including the head-to-tail arrangement and body segmentations. The proposed model exhibits exceptional performance on multiple public datasets featuring a diverse range of full-body images of intestinal parasites from humans, birds, and mammals.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of joint stock and capital processes that follow interrelated Markov chains with varying regimes, and which feature jumps and continuous components. We propose simulating these processes as a joint stochastic system that can be efficiently solved using Monte Carlo methods. The approximation is particularly accurate in the vicinity of the regime-switching regime boundaries. We demonstrate this technique's viability by applying it to two industries - insurance and finance - specifically in the areas of proportional reinsurance and dynamic trading strategies.

This study introduces a unique approach to optimize the performance of Quadrotor drones through a two-part system incorporating a Genetic Filter and a Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm PIDA. We first fine-tune the current PID controller with a genetic algorithm to create an optimal generalized PID (G-PID) and then integrate this with the PIDA to produce the proposed PIDA controller. We also incorporate an observer known as the Genetic Filter to detect system uncertainties in the proposed controller framework. We utilize Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm to accelerate optimization and enhance computational efficiency. We have tested the proposed system on air-borne vehicles, demonstrating its ability to achieve accurate trajectory tracking with enhanced stability and reliability.

A review is presented focusing on the significance of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions.
Key points involving the QCD chiral symmetry, the determination of low-energy constants, the partial waves of $s$, $p$, and $d$, the branching ratios of $\pi \pi$ scattering, the properties of baryon resonances, and the Baryon $\sigma$ term are the primary topics.
The analysis also considers recent findings from lattice QCD calculations, the development of the "big data" analysis, and the impact of the $\pi\pi$ scattering amplitude on chiral perturbation theory.
The review highlights how the constraints imposed by the analyticity of amplitudes impose stringent limits on the validity of the low-energy expansion and the values of coupling constants.
Furthermore, it examines the effects of chiral loops on low-energy constants, particularly in the $s$ and $p$-waves.
We also investigate the constraints that unitarity places on $s$-, $p$-, and $d$-wave amplitudes, the discovery of the $\sigma$ pole in $\ell s$-wave amplitudes, and how it relates to the masses and decay widths of low-mass scalar resonances.
We also explore various approaches to isolate low-energy constants from partial waves, the mass dependence of coupling constants, and the effects of variations in the quark mass on these parameters.
We also investigate various methods for extracting partial wave

Over the past decade, various complex machines have been assembled to detect and analyze particle collisions within the Large Hadron Collider. Among them, the CMS detector plays a vital role in studying these events, particularly those involving protons, by recording and localizing these collisions with remarkable precision, taking advantage of a silicon pixel detection system. Although a full-scale CMS detector is still under development, the CMS collaboration recently built and tested a pilot module known as a 'blade,' which served as a learning tool for building the ultimate CMS detector's pixel system during its development phase. With a limited number of blades constructed so far, it's crucial to thoroughly analyze and understand their data accurately before proceeding further. It's also essential to understand how particle interactions can affect these blades and cause damage to them. In this context, we have designed and implemented a novel technique to analyze particle collisions using a specific software tool called 'Geant4.' This analysis aims to examine a reconstructed particle collision in a simulated environment, which closely matches a real particle collision in a simulated environment, to validate and confirm that a particle collision in a simulated environment is authentic.

Active galactic nuclei found in galaxies located 0.5 billion light years behind us are known to be similar in nature to those in the early stages of the universe. Understanding the characteristics of these galaxies is vital in studying black hole growth and active galactic nuclei. The Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey will provide detailed images of active galactic nuclei host galaxies, drawing a comparison between them and blue galaxy populations at the same distance. Determining the blueness of these host galaxies is complicated by the presence of AGN, and we employ a machine learning model to classify blue galaxies versus AGN in the z < 1 sample. Training the model using data from the Wide Survey and comparing it to blue galaxy populations allows us to identify structures within the sample. We draw comparisons between machine learning classifications and established relationships between blue galaxies and AGN at lower redshift levels.

Nuclear short-range correlations are studied from both microscopic and phenomenological standpoints.  A non-relativistic effective field theory (EFT) framework is utilized to analyze correlation structures in finite nuclei.  Given the highly oscillatory nature of wave functions associated with short-range correlations, their representation within nucleus-specific phase spaces is challenging.  To address this issue, the momentum distribution and Feynman spectral function are derived for relatively soft external probes, revealing a distinct, non-overlapping relationship between employed probes and virtual transitions involving short-range correlated nucleon pairs.  This finding substantiates the efficacy of such "soft" probes for isolating short-range correlation effects during collision events.

Deep learning algorithms are highly effective in processing diverse inputs, including those with complex data, but can also incorporate advanced pre-processing techniques that map the real realm into the complex domain for enhanced algorithm performance. Currently, complex numbers are treated as pairs of real numbers in deep learning frameworks, resulting in increased computational costs and simplified computations. To resolve this issue, we propose an innovative approach to define complex domain equality in deep graph frameworks, enabling a more precise co-domain match between complex-valued neural networks and significantly reduced computational costs. This solution is successfully demonstrated through experiments on machine classification tasks, showcasing the efficiency of defining complex number equality through co-domain exploration in deep graph frameworks.

The non-linear evolution of the gluon distribution within the proton or nucleus at high density causes the saturation of cross sections for Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS). One of the most telling characteristics of saturation theory is geometrical scaling, implying that the deep inelastic scattering cross sections depend on a specific variable, $\tau = x_x x_0/Q_\lambda^2\alpha_s(\lambda^2)/2$, across different values of $Q^2$ and $x_B$. Empirical data from various sources, including electron-proton, electron-nucleus, and proton-nucleus collisions, demonstrate the effectiveness of this scaling variable in describing data. Furthermore, similar geometrical scaling is observed in the baryon production multiplicity data in proton-nucleon and massive ion collisions at a range of collision energies. These findings suggest that geometrical scaling serves as a reliable indicator for approaching saturation in the proton-nucleon collision system at LHC energies and may suggest that saturation scales are already being reached at top collision energies.

The low-metallicity star field is widely regarded as the birthplace of various anomalous light element patterns observed in certain populations, such as the first-generation members of globular clusters and the CN-binary stars. In the absence of amorphous star surfaces, amplitudes in spectral lines are diminished, allowing for the identification of two distinct groups based on their chemical composition. However, the exact number of these populations is yet to be fully understood. In an effort to gain a deeper understanding, we have analyzed a sample of 111 low-metallicity stars from the VVDS-GTO catalogue, taking into account their spectral line variations and structural differences. We have discovered that variations in spectral line amplitudes are not only linked to differences in nitrogen and carbon but are also influenced by factors such as mass and temperature. We have found that 40 out of 111 stars in the sample, which possess surface masses of less than 0.8 solar masses, do not conform to the established populations, suggesting the presence of a third population in these low-metallicity systems.

Machine learning models are widely used in various domains, including finance, healthcare, and education, where they are applied to predictive challenges. However, the reliance on these models poses significant risks, particularly in critical decision-making scenarios, highlighting the need for robust tools to assess their performance. Our study introduces a surgical toolbox method for measuring the influence of individual features on machine learning predictions and demonstrates its application in evaluating financial literacy predictions made using the FFCS dataset.

This research introduces SQUID, a framework allowing SQUIDs to be trained in much the same way neurons are, enabling the SQUID framework to be utilized as an accelerator for developing quantum machine intelligence systems. It achieves this by leveraging quantum computing to create SQUIDs that can be trained efficiently, robustly, and adaptively. Each SQUID is composed of a Josephson junction, a nanoscale inductor-capacitor circuit that exhibits superconducting properties. Within the SQUID framework, parameters are represented by the magnetic flux applied to the Josephson junction and can be trained by adjusting this flux in response to specific input signals. Furthermore, the SQUID framework capitalizes on the inherent capabilities of Josephson junctions, which are highly sensitive to external electromagnetic fields and capable of detecting and processing multi-photon states. This inherent property enables the SQUID framework to interact with the surrounding environment, collect data, and learn from it.

This study focuses on warped product pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds within the framework of almost contact manifolds, where we derive a crucial condition for their warping functions and derive a key theorem that can be used to measure their degree of warping. A significant finding shows that when such a submanifold has a time-like principal normal, its warping function remains constant and therefore does not exist in the warped product space. To provide a concrete example, we have also given a specific instance of such a warped product submanifold. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that when the spacelike pointwise semi-inclined submanifold becomes timelike pointwise inclined, a key warping function becomes constant in every instance, and we have proven that its warping function is invariant under these conditions.

The research involves analyzing the detection capabilities of color centers, such as those in diamond, for identifying low-energy nuclear movements in order to develop a new generation of low-energy particle detectors that can identify dark matter and other properties through mechanical forces in a variety of settings, such as those involving solid states. This work outlines the experimental methods used to measure the levels of radiation damage caused by nuclear collisions in samples of colorful defects. Since its discovery, color centers have become an extensively researched area of physics, encompassing photon emission, quantum memory, and a wide range of optical properties that change with temperature. Although the exact nature of the light produced by these defects is still being studied, recent research has allowed scientists to accurately measure and understand their properties in detail. By examining the patterns of light produced when exposed to different types of radiation, such as neutron and gamma rays, scientists have been able to identify and quantify the levels of damage caused by these defects.

We conduct a thorough examination of a type of artificial molecule, consisting of multiple interconnected particles, exposed to an activity-based variation. Through detailed kinetic analysis, we demonstrate how thermal motion interacts with this chemical environment, resulting in a type of effective force. Our analytical model successfully correlates numerical data generated from detailed simulations. Moreover, we show that this type of artificial life form can exhibit behaviors typically seen in non-living matter subjected to similar external influences, exhibiting single-particle characteristics. Notably, this artificial life form can exhibit behaviors typically seen in traditional Brownian particles, effectively experiencing an environment that is uniform but anisotropic, resulting in the appearance of an effective magnetic field. Finally, we discuss significant differences between the behavior of artificial molecules and traditional Brownian particles subjected to the same type of chemical environment.

Investigating spectral patterns in extended wave functions, specifically magnetorotons, reveals a underlying set of integer rules that describe their energies. This research generalizes previously found patterns to encompass all fractional quantum Hall states with non-zero spin. Building upon this, it individualizes previously collective characteristics like $\nu=1/3$ and $\nu=1/2$, resulting in two or three prominent magnetoroton modes. For each spectral pattern, an associated sum rule exists. This new understanding of spectral patterns offers fresh insights into the underlying sum rules and the sum rules into the sum rules themselves.

Identifying and analyzing epidemic clusters within networks is a critical task in understanding outbreaks. We introduce a new approach using geometry to uncover nested cluster structures in networks harboring artificial and real-generated outbreak data. Notably, our method performs as well as existing techniques on real data and is computationally efficient and straightforward to implement.

Developing accurate CMB maps is a crucial task in experiments like CMB-SAD. Currently, the common approach of using maximum likelihood estimation to estimate the CMB amplitude and brightness temperature of sources has a significant drawback: it tends to produce maps with artificially reduced source amplitudes and exaggerated CMB patterns around those sources. This phenomenon can be mistaken for primordial magnetic eddies, even though it is merely an artifact of point source subtraction. We investigate the reasons behind this and show that the issue stems from the fact that this estimation method is not robust to changes in the number of sources. We propose a solution by incorporating the experimental noise into the analysis and present an analytical method for this approach.

Deep goal-conditioned reinforcement learning models are designed to find solutions for a variety of tasks based solely on student's verbal instructions and are widely regarded as a more intuitive and accessible form of human interaction compared to command-based instruction learning. Nevertheless, our research demonstrates that current deep goal-conditioned instruction-learning models are hindered by a significant issue known as referential ambiguity, which poses a severe challenge to their effectiveness. In essence, these models struggle due to their inclination to generalize learned skills in a rigid and sequential manner, often leading to the execution of tasks in an incorrect order when presented with verbally instructed guidance. We utilize a simulation-based robotic experiment as a case study to demonstrate the complexities associated with this problem in real-world applications and illustrate its impact on the performance of state-of-the-art instruction-learning models. Moreover, we offer novel approaches to mitigate and potentially resolve challenges related to referential ambiguity, including order-agnostic teacher-student architectures and the development of a generalized order-agnostic teacher that outperforms current models by accurately executing verbally instructed skills with considerable accuracy across a range of 50 distinct robotic tasks with various levels of complexities and variations.

We propose a fundamental quantum imaging technique, inspired by Grover's algorithm, which provides an intuitive and imageable interpretation of quantum operations as spatial transformations. Either by direct physical implementation of quantum circuits or by leveraging theoretical device models, our method enables a precise mathematical illustration of complex open-quantum system dynamics. Focusing on single-qubit channels as an example, our approach is validated with various open-quasi particle models, including a chaotic Drude model with single-phonon dissipation and a non-Markovian Leaky Quantum Dot model, both of which were successfully applied to reconstruct the unitary evolution of the system dynamics up to its non-unitary decay point.

For planar convex bodies, we derive sharp inequalities linking the Cheeger constant with various means, along with related concepts. These inequalities ultimately lead to precise estimates for the Cheeger constant. Additionally, we establish sharp inequalities comparing the Cheeger constant and first non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian with Dirichlet boundary conditions. All obtained inequalities are optimal.

This study explores optimal path design for aerial drones to carry out tasks that have a specific time window for completion. We introduce a new model, incorporate constraints to account for the time-sensitive nature of tasks, and derive equations to minimize energy consumption. A heuristic algorithm is developed to solve the model and allows for testing under various conditions. Results indicate the model can achieve significant energy savings compared to paths generated by existing algorithms.

The instability of interacting bilayer graphite at low energies is studied using a renormalization group method, where the analysis focuses on how the fine structure alpha and Hubbard U constants evolve. The consideration of multiple possible low-energy fluctuations in bilayer graphite reveals that it depends on whether electrons occupy even or odd orbital states. Alpha decreases while increasing the energy scale and a specific two-current interaction prevents instability, whereas the Hubbard U increases and instability arises unless Hubbard coupling is absent, leading to possible magnetic instability. Comparisons with single-layer and double-QS experiments reveal significant discrepancies, suggesting that the latter involves unusual interactions. The study indicates that instability may be prevented by electrons occupying states near the interface due to strong electric fields applied during experiments.

The behavior of Sc2TbN@C80 on h-BN/Ni(111) was studied through high and low-temperature X-ray photoemission spectroscopy, revealing that the compound adopts two distinct molecular conformations. The first conformation remains stable at room temperature but is unstable under low-temperature conditions, whereas the second conformation persists at both temperatures. The underlying cause of these conformations has been identified as the dual peak structure of the Ni 3d band and how it interacts with the doped electrons in C2-symmetric fullerenes, resulting in conformations with differing binding energy. The observed shift in binding energy for the second conformation at low temperatures supports a doping mechanism.

Emerging IoT applications demand secure encryption in resource-constrained environments. This challenge is addressed by a new CP-SE algorithm that balances security and energy efficiency. Compared to established schemes, the CP-SE algorithm achieves enhanced security while significantly reducing energy consumption and increasing data transmission speed by a factor of 1.7 times. This is accomplished through a novel encryption technique involving chaotic maps on the IoT device and on cloud servers for cross-prime encryption, allowing the CP-SE algorithm to accommodate large data sets and high processing capabilities. Furthermore, the CP-SE algorithm's lightweight nature enables efficient encryption of small, embedded IoT devices. A simulation using MATLAB on the ARM Cortex-M4 processor demonstrates the algorithm's feasibility and superior performance.

The Ramsey measurement technique, widely employed in atom interferometry to assess Ramsey's inductive signal, suffers from low efficiency due to unoptimized experimental parameters. This measurement process involves multiple sequential steps, including preparing the atomic ensemble, executing the microwave pulse sequence, and detecting the resulting signal. A traditional approach to measuring the Ramsey signal involves pre-defining the entire sequence of experimental run parameters before the experiment begins. However, this method may not always be practical, especially when the required ensemble size is large. Our research introduces an innovative strategy to optimize the adaptive sequence of experiments in real-time during the measurement process. Our approach utilizes Bayesian probability theory to determine the most efficient sequence of experiments that will yield the most accurate estimation of the atomic ensemble's phase angle. Our numerical results indicate that the outcome of our adaptive measurement will have significantly higher precision compared to traditional methods with the same ensemble size. Furthermore, the accuracy of our adaptive measurement will converge towards the precision of the traditional method as the number of experiments increases. Our adaptive measurement technique will be particularly useful in atom interferometry, where it will enable more efficient real-time measurements of magnetic field fluctuations with larger ensembles and at lower costs.

Network centrality metrics assess node importance by analyzing connectivity and inequality relationships between nodes. We develop Gromov centrality, a novel metric, which quantifies the distance sum of a node based on a non-metric distance determined by the network adjacency matrix. We demonstrate that Gromov centrality is highly scalable, capable of processing large networks efficiently. Its properties enable application across various network types and we showcase its effectiveness in different fields and scale. Finally, we demonstrate Gromov centrality's ability to predict characteristics and behaviors in target networks and compare it favorably to established centrality measures.

A symmetric spherical model of gravitation features a metric with elements dependent on R(r), a function describing the gravitational potential's spherical symmetry.  At distances significantly larger than R(r), a specific limit emerges where R(r) behaves inversely proportional to r, a characteristic similar to Newtonian gravity.  This limit is associated with constant values of R_0, a similar effect to the Schwarzschild radius, and a similar influence on a test particle.  Furthermore, a symmetric model of gravity also results in a similar relationship to R_0, and a similar effect to the time dilation around a massive object.

This paper investigates the relationship between various equivalence concepts for bundles of matrix operators, focusing on strict equivalence as a primary framework. We establish strict equivalence as a more rigorous form of isomorphism for such equivalence theories. We investigate bundle isomorphisms arising from groups of operators that preserve matrix form and demonstrate their connection to operator factorizations. We delve into the theory of operator bundles formed by $p$-divisible operators, a widely studied area of research, providing new insights into their structure, including a classification under strict equivalence and a classification under equivalent theory of isomorphism. We also explore related topics such as $p$-root factorizations of operators and their relationship to operator bundles.

This article proposes a novel concept of topological T-duality for twisted cylinders $M_\theta$ by 
focusing on their K-theory properties. K-theory data for arbitrary open or closed intervals on circles rotated by an irrational angle $\theta$ are calculated and used to establish a concrete type of T-duality in topological K-theory, particularly in cases without closure. The theory's validity is demonstrated through the successful application to key examples in topological K-theory, including those by Freed-Hopkins-Lenhard-Witten and Carlsson-Goldstein.

We develop an efficient algorithm to represent any given metric space with a specific property (being a minor-free or being a subset of a specific graph's minor) in a specific form (having a certain tree-width-related measure less than a certain value times a specific value to the first power less than a given value to the third power) in subexponential time. The form involves representing the space as being a subset of a specific tree-structured network, where the maximum distance between any two points on the network is limited by a specific value raised to a specific power less than a given value and the network itself being based on a specific tree structure. The tree structure includes additional edge labels drawn from a specific set of values, and we show that such a representation can be constructed in subexponential time. Furthermore, we prove that this algorithm works by leveraging known results from a specific area of mathematics (related to graph minors and planar graphs) to derive a specific upper bound on the maximum distance between any two points on the network and the size of the set of values and demonstrate that these bounds can be computed efficiently in subexponential time.

For C^2-smooth, discrete-time systems that are strongly monotonic, we have found that near any non-fixed point, invariant set, we can linearize the system. This leads to a classification of the system's smooth prevalent behavior into three distinct categories near such points. These categories are equivalent to prevalent categories of the system's dynamics near any non-fixed point, any invariant manifold, and any fixed point respectively. We identified that the quadratic normal form exhibits prevalence in the second category, as does strong saddle-singular source and strong saddle-saddle configuration within the third category. Conversely, within the first category, linear systems and higher-order strong normal forms exhibit prevalence. These findings for C^2-strongly monotonic discrete-time systems extend existing previous research and provide significant insights into prevalent behavior for a broader class of such systems.

Quantum computers have the potential to be vulnerable to various forms of noise, making them unreliable for certain complex problems. In contrast, the variational approach has the advantage of combining quantum computing and classical computing to overcome this issue, albeit at the cost of requiring a substantial number of quantum circuit executions for complex problems. Our team has developed an innovative variation of the variational approach called QE-BVA, which aims to speed up the process and reduce the number of required executions by an order of magnitude. The QE-BVA approach simplifies the quantum circuit significantly and leverages it for a more efficient optimization process. By comparing the performance of QE-BVA against traditional VQE and a previous variant called EVA, our research demonstrates that it offers notable advantages for solving complex problems with limited quantum resources, providing it with greater robustness and efficiency in these contexts.

A key component of deep learning systems, especially those based on variational autoencoders, is the encoder. Traditionally, researchers approximate encoder outputs using mean estimates, but there has been limited exploration of using MAP estimates instead. This study provides evidence that MAP estimates can yield superior results due to reduced representation estimation error resulting from lower posterior collapse. Furthermore, this work introduces techniques to directly estimate the required components for MAP estimates through regression, and these methods achieve comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art.

The discrepancy between early measurements of the expansion rate and late measurements of it might be resolved by adding an extra phase to the duration of the inflationary period. Introducing a stiff period in the inflationary model causes primordial gravitational waves to increase the present density of gravitational waves, which could be detected as a continuous stochastic background. Researchers have found that even low-energy levels of this inflation, which could be confirmed by the Laser Interferometer Telescope, could address the discrepancy between early and late measurements of the expansion rate.

A survey of the molecule carbon monosulfide ($^{32}$CO$^{34}$S) in comet C/2015 ER61 using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) was conducted, resulting in the detection of this molecule in the comet. The survey aimed to analyze this molecule across a range of distances from the Sun, expanding upon earlier observations made by the European Southern Observatory's Atacama Large Millimeter Telescope (ALMA) at Mauna Kea. The observations were made using the ALMA Atacama Compact Array, which allowed for higher resolution imaging. The results showed that $^{32}$CO$^{34}$S exists throughout the comet's outgassing activity, with no evidence of a nucleus-based source. The molecule's distribution is consistent with its parent, carbon monosulfide ($^{12}$C$^{32}$S), suggesting a link between the two. The study also observed a moderate increase in $^{32}$CO$^{34}$S emission as the comet approached the Sun, which could be due to variations in the comet's activity or changes in the environment surrounding the comet.

This research introduces an unsupervised, end-to-end speech synthesis model that operates without requiring labeled audio data or linguistic information for training. Unlike its supervised counterparts, this model achieves high efficiency by training a compact encoder to generate a concise encoder matrix from audio input alone. Moreover, by leveraging a pre-trained external language model, the model produces enhanced speaker representations, allowing it to generate speech without fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the model's efficacy in achieving comparable synthesis quality to supervised methods and demonstrate its efficiency in cross-speaker and cross-language reconstruction of high-quality speech, particularly from non-verbal vocal sounds.

This study focuses on a type of dark energy known as essence energy, a concept first introduced by Panos Papadopoulos and later renamed by Harko in 2007 as essence energy, characterized by the presence of an essence field that interacts with a scalar field to influence cosmic dynamics. To explore its effect on the universe, researchers have employed the principles of holographic dark energy (HDE) as part of the essence model. To identify the appropriate cutoff parameter for the HDE within the essence model, this work utilizes the fractional free energy density of matter to calculate the stability of a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) universe within the context of the essence model. To gain deeper insight into the essence model's dynamics, this research expresses the essence field's contribution to the total energy momentum tensor as an essential component of the total energy momentum tensor. Consequently, this component is referred to as the essence energy density, a term distinct from energy density associated with a scalar field in HDE. Furthermore, this work examines the impact of an essential coupling constant on the universe's expansion rate and solves the resulting differential equation for a power law scale factor, a necessary step in understanding the universe's expansion dynamics. To assess the model's stability, this research applies the slow-roll parameters and investigates the stability of FRW cosmology within the context of the essence model. Lastly, this work calculates the stability of FRW cosmology by using the slow-roll parameters and examining the model

Multi-objective non-linear optimization problems are common in real-world applications and often feature complex constraints and objective functions. Various evolutionary algorithms, such as those with insertion operators, have been applied to their solution, including its use in real options analysis. Researchers proposed a novel multi-objective optimization algorithm, combining NSGA-II and insertion operators, to tackle such problems. Its performance was tested and compared to existing approaches, such as multiple-run genetic algorithms and insertion algorithm methods. The results indicated that the hybrid algorithm produced superior results in terms of solution diversity, while outperforming insertion algorithms in computational efficiency. The comparison with multi-objective genetic algorithms revealed comparable solution quality with the advantage of lower processing time for the former. The efficacy of this approach was demonstrated using the problem of real options for a company planning to invest in hydrogen production technology.

We refine the concepts of internal completeness and integral completeness for Lie groups within synthetic differential geometry, then demonstrate their equivalence for connected Lie groups within the standard real-toothpick model and the basic $K[[\tau]][[t]]$ model.

The integration of cyberinfrastructure and data science has significantly improved research efficiency in the health sciences by streamlining collaboration and communication within communities. However, this advancement has also raised concerns over security, privacy, and data security, necessitating a comprehensive approach involving technical solutions, policies, and legal frameworks. This paper examines a security framework that utilizes user credentials and project access controls along with security, privacy, and audit measures to protect and manage sensitive health sciences data during sharing through a centralized cyberinfrastructure platform.

Aspect-based aspect sentiment analysis aims to identify the sentiment towards specific aspects and also assess the overall sentiment of the text. In our study, we notice that the overall sentiment captures an important dimension of the aspects and helps in understanding the overall emotion. To capture this implicit emotion, we propose a new pre-training approach using a supervised method that involves a data augmentation strategy to improve the robustness of our model. The proposed approach learns the implicit emotion by designing a simple yet effective network that makes use of a general domain dictionary of emotions. The overall sentiment information is incorporated into our model through a cross-attention mechanism that facilitates cross-text and cross-aspect attention. Experimental results on three aspect-based sentiment analysis datasets show that our approach effectively captures implicit emotion information and significantly outperforms the current best performance on two of the datasets.

We examine the indirect effect in a cohort where individuals are screened and selected using rare-disease case-control methods, and whose population includes a binary variable of interest as well as a binary mediator. To accurately estimate individual indirect effects, we developed a generalized version of the product of probability formula, accommodating case-control studies. Next, we investigated whether these indirect effects can be represented through a weighted regression model. To tackle the challenges of covariate imbalances between study cases and controls, and to minimize information loss due to sampling, we proposed a two-stage estimation technique utilizing case-control sampling, and specifically the generalized estimating equations approach. Furthermore, we investigated the asymptotic properties of our estimator and formulated a corresponding hypothesis test for assessing marginal indirect effects. We validated our theoretical findings through detailed simulation experiments and实际应用案例研究.

This study tackles secure communication in multiuser networks that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces and suffer from hardware impairments.
We examine a system that transmits confidential information to two distinct users while preventing an unauthorized user from accessing it.
To optimize a convex problem, we reformulate the original non-convex problem by utilizing second-order cone constraints and then apply successive convex approximation to find an approximate optimal solution.
We further refine the proposed solution by leveraging the mirror descent method and demonstrating the mirroring effect to converge towards optimality.
Our results show that this scheme achieves better performance than conventional methods under similar conditions.
Additionally, our study considers various impairment levels and signal-to-noise ratios, while analyzing the proposed scheme using two different algorithms.
Our simulations confirm that this scheme effectively enhances the secrecy rate, particularly in scenarios involving low impairment levels.

Our approach to a widely studied cognitive ability, executive function, involves leveraging contrastive value estimation for hindsight summarization. We interpret executive function as a multi-task framework centered on contrastive value learning, which facilitates task sequencing and summarization. By casting these tasks as a joint objective of next-token prediction, we develop a scalable training strategy for resampling and reevaluating perceptions. Moreover, our framework enables the pursuit of implicit state estimation for decision-making tasks. Leveraging a large language model, we demonstrate the potential of our approach to mitigate bias in perception and enhance decision-making in simulated environments through resampling, relabeling, and reevaluating perceptions.

Investigations of energetic particles in the inner solar system have provided insights into the mechanisms and energy sources of solar and interplanetary space. However, understanding these processes in the region closest to the sun, specifically within 0.3 astronomical units, has been limited, largely due to observations from the Parker Solar Probe mission beginning in 2018. The initial findings from the probe reveal characteristic patterns in energetic particle events, such as solar breeze events, with distinct features extending down to 0.26 astronomical units. These events, which make up a significant majority of the events observed so far, are primarily composed of protons with secondary electrons and helium ions, showing relatively uniform energy spectra across the observed distance. The overall particle density decreases in a power-law relationship with distance from the sun, with the power varying depending on the type of particle involved, thereby offering new insights into the region where these events originate.

In a quantum context, we establish a connection between actions of discrete groups on C*-algebras and quantum group actions, demonstrating that every action arising from a discrete group's cofinite dual, referred to as a principal bundle action, can be embedded within a quantum group action of equivalent properties. We also introduce a method to develop noncommutative versions of classical geometric shapes based on their underlying algebraic structures.

The study of cardinal characteristics of the continuum mainly focuses on infinity, but 
sometimes examining finite values offers new insights. This paper delves into two 
such instances: the ultrafilter number $\mathfrak{u}$ and a previously unexplored 
characteristic, defined as the nearly disjointness number $\mathcal{N}$. An 
in-depth investigation reveals a nearly disjointness number $\mathcal{N}$ can be 
strictly less than its disjointness counterpart $\mathcal{D}$, and establishes 
the inequality $\mathcal{N} \leq \mathfrak{p} < \mathfrak{b}$.

This investigation focuses on observing the phenomenon of fast light in an optomechanical system influenced by the $q$-deformation parameter through nonlinearity and in the presence of a telegrapher's model medium. By utilizing this medium, researchers aim to achieve high-speed communication systems with elevated clarity and minimal noise. To investigate fast and slow light phenomena, scholars employed the Heisenberg transfer matrix method and analyzed the energy spectral density and group velocity of the electromagnetic fields within the system. Additionally, researchers proposed models based on Lorentzian and Debye models to amplify and process fast light and evaluated the effectiveness and efficiency of these models.

In the two rotors model for supersymmetric nuclear structure, negative parity R-parity states are tested against real experimental data. These states show a unique property where they don't mix with other R-parity states but are coupled to a rotor. While most R-parity states exhibit an oscillating behavior, some do not, indicating an anomaly. This anomaly is specifically observed in the first adverse R-parity state, which is found to have a minimal coupling to the rotated partner of its parent nucleus in certain isomers, but is strongly coupled in others, illustrating the model's rich structure.

A new cell-mean based neural network method is developed for solving hyperbolic and parabolic PDEs. This method utilizes a neural network to approximate the spatial averages of solutions over computational cells. A notable advantage of this method is that it requires no initial guess for starting the iterative process. The method's stability in the hyperbolic case and accuracy in the parabolic case are theoretically proven. Furthermore, we demonstrate through numerical experiments that the method achieves optimal convergence rates in the $L_{\infty}$-norm and can effectively resolve discontinuities while preserving sharp shock waves.

The ALICE experiment at the LHC is focused on studying the properties of the quark-gluon plasma and the nucleon-nucleon interactions in various collision environments. The experiment is enhancing its capabilities beyond LHC Run 3 with the arrival of the FELIX upgrade. This involves the installation of the Zero Degree Calorimeter and the upgraded Forward Zero Degree Calorimeter, as well as increasing the capabilities of the Central Zero Point and adapting the detector layout for the beam halo scan during FELICE beam test runs following LHC Run 3 and beyond.

The Unruh effect describes how an accelerating observer perceives the Minkowski vacuum as a thermal state, with their past and future light cones separated by a Rindler horizon. A groundbreaking study proposed a way to observe the Unruh effect's entanglement-based approach by introducing a 'time-like' version where future and past light cones are compared across the horizon. This 'timer' would gain a geometric phase due to the tim-like Unruh phenomenon, with the phase's value determined by the observer's acceleration. This framework provides an alternative explanation of the Berry phase's origin, combining insights from the Unruh effect and holonomy concepts to explain quantum phase changes in parallel with existing theories such as those proposed by Wilczek and Zee.

To effectively detect and respond to critical incidents, researchers have been
investigating automatic incident detection and extraction systems. Current systems
primarily focus on English, but real-world applications necessitate support for
various languages. Existing research on other languages is limited, hindering
development of multilingual incident extraction systems. We propose a multilingual
dataset featuring real Twitter incidents and show through experiments that
optimizing pre-trained models can yield improved extraction performance in
languages beyond Arabic, Chinese, and English. The dataset is available online
for further research into multilingual incident extraction and mining studies.

We derive a global relationship between the Chern forms of two global vector spaces with the same dimensions but the area measures provided by two different metrics, one inducing the other, under the assumption that the area difference is the derivative of a global object by that metric's area, leading to a precise mathematical equivalence that determines the degree of possible variation in characteristic forms and the Morse inequality for global vector spaces under global transformation.

Our analysis examines the spectral-timing properties of the stellar breeze in the high-state variant of the binary system Cyg X-1. Utilizing XMM-Newton data, we have achieved the most detailed understanding of this system to date, revealing an increase in the power of low-frequency timing signals as it transitions to an harder state. Analyzing the high-state variant, we have identified distinct characteristics of the soft and hard states. In the high-state variant, we have found evidence of temporal variations in the power of a specific temporal signal, which aligns with expectations based on the accretion rate fluctuations. Inference suggests that a significant proportion of the temporal signal originates from the stellar breeze material, which falls onto the surface of the black hole, thereby contributing to its timing signals.

The study of a specific ether-like modification of N=1 super-Yang-Mills theory is conducted within a thermal environment. By calculating the thermal masses of gauge bosons using one-loop self-energy corrections, we discover that the non-zero ether-like coupling yields non-zero thermal masses even when the gauge coupling is minimal. Additionally, the theory's effective potential is evaluated in a SU(2) context to analyze spontaneous symmetry breaking possibilities within a high-temperature environment.

To effectively understand text, two critical components need to be
effectively integrated: grammatical structure and word meanings. Our new
approach efficiently combines these aspects under a unified framework, enabling
the parsing of syntax and semantics simultaneously. This innovative method
requires minimal additional data and is capable of being applied to any existing
parser without the need for retraining. By introducing the concept of universal
semirings, we demonstrate how to concurrently process different semantic parsers
for syntax and semantic meaning while maintaining computational efficiency.
The proposed approach was tested using the state-of-the-art parser MaltParser and
the logic parser DL-R, showcasing its ability to produce accurate syntax trees and
conceptual representations without the need for additional tuning.

We conducted simulations of magnetized disks formed following the collision of two neutron stars, where the disk has a radius of approximately 15 km and an initial magnetic field strength of $10^{-9}$ G. The magnetic field was developed through the amplification mechanism known as the Goldreich-Flynn-Ward process, occurring during the merger process. Our simulations indicate that the disintegration of the merged remnant leads to the rapid expansion of the disk within the first second of its evolution. The expanded disk drives the magnetically-fed outflow generated by the magnetorotational instability, a phenomenon characterized by a mass outflow rate of approximately $10^{-2}$ solar masses per year and the specific morphology known as a "jet-clump." The jet-clump morphology arises from the interaction between the magnetically-fed outflow and the surrounding medium, driven by the standing shocks that accelerate and thermalize the outflow as it exits the disk. The jet-clump morphology is further influenced by the magnetic field strength and rotation rate of the merged remnant, as well as its remnant's mass. The results of these simulations suggest that the magnetically-fed outflow generated by a disk has a characteristic temperature of several keV and a luminosity of approximately $10^{44}$ ergs per second, potentially explaining the thermal component of several "magnetar-like" postmerger transients. In a comprehensive study, researchers used deep imaging data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam to analyze the morphological characteristics of mass-limited galaxies from three datasets with varying redshift ranges. By specifically focusing on tidal features in galaxies with mass greater than 10^11 solar masses, they found that early-type galaxies at redshifts 0.1-0.3 possess a 10% greater fraction of these features compared to their peers beyond redshift 0.3. This difference is approximately 20% and corresponds to a differential star formation rate of the order of 10^-3 per 10^9 solar years. This observed trend in the fraction of galaxies with tidal features aligns with expectations from merger simulations, which suggest a significant increase in merger rates between redshifts 0.2 and 0.3. By contrasting these findings with late-type galaxies, which also show a similar increase in merger rates, the researchers highlight the significant role of tidal interactions in shaping massive galaxies and suggest further investigation into other processes involved in galaxy formation.

A theoretical paper explores bipolar supermassive stars using the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation, revealing an opposing effect to the stars' rotation. Bates-Langmuir's classical theory predicts a centrifugal force pushing gas outward due to the rotation, but the new theory establishes a gravitational effect pulling it in the opposite direction. Researchers identify an Euler equation-based pressure corresponding to the directional gravity, showing increased repulsive effects with heightened rotational speeds. At critical velocities, the star's surface pressure balances itself against external space.

We have studied the Chandra Deep Field South for hard X-ray and gamma-ray emission in close proximity to four known FRBs, which are characterized by their repetitive nature. Our research aimed to detect any associated X-ray or gamma-ray bursts. Using 2012-2013 Swift-XRT data, we set the upper limits on the 2-10 keV X-ray luminosity of each FRB source. Our observations have not found any evidence of steady X-ray luminosity, or the switching on of X-ray emission within the 0.1-100 s time window following the FRB bursts. Our research has also set the upper limits on the 511 keV photon flux from the 4 FRB sources, which has not detected any emission. Our Swift-ATGAT observations have not detected any time-delayed hard X-ray or gamma-ray emission from the 4 FRB sources within the 2012-2013 data. Our research has set the upper limits on the 3-30 keV photon flux of any simultaneous X-ray emission from the FRB sources, and 50 keV photon flux of any delayed X-ray emission. Our research has not detected any evidence of the 2-10 keV or 50 keV photon flux of any simultaneous or time-delayed X-ray emission from the FRB sources, which has not been found.
