For large-scale tensor data, low-rank approximation through methods like the tensor singular value decomposition (TSD) is crucial for data compression and noise reduction. This paper proposes a randomized algorithm for efficient TSD approximation, allowing multiple passes to enhance results when the number of passes is unknown. A key assumption underpinning this technique is that the underlying tensor follows a factor model where latent variables exhibit weak dependence. Numerical experiments demonstrate that increased numbers of passes yield better outcomes in approximating the tensor's eigen-spectrum.

As more applications involve processing and representing data as dynamic graphs, 
it's essential to efficiently update graph neural networks without retraining 
them from scratch, which is particularly challenging when the input graphs change continuously over time. 
This difficulty arises because traditional embedding techniques are designed for static graphs only, 
resulting in information loss when applied to evolving graphs. 
This study explores the area of embedding evolving graphs, examining how time-series 
and network data evolve over time and the methods used to capture these changes, 
followed by a discussion on the new issues and open questions that evolving graphs present, 
concluding with an analysis of existing datasets and a comparison of their properties.

To investigate the structure of super- and hyper-halo nuclei, the microscopic cluster model is applied with a focus on $^7$H. The model treats $^3$H and four neutrons as the constituent particles and incorporates the dynamic nature of these neutrons using the Crandall distribution. The calculated energy and size properties of $^7$H match available experimental data using a specific parameter value that also yields a root mean square neutron correlation with shell configurations. This parameter value suggests an excited $^3$H state with spin and parity 3/2+, indicating the presence of spatial asymmetry in the neutron matter. The findings support the interpretation of $^7$H as a neutron-rich droplet with a core consisting of $^3$H, surrounded by four neutrons.

We focus on the Nirenberg problem for half spheres with curved boundaries, seeking solutions to equation -u^{\frac{n+2}{n-2}} = \lambda \ h(u) \delta^{-\alpha} for parameters λ, α > 0 on the sphere product space. Specifically, it has been established that for a chosen λ > 0 and α > 0, there exists a function f in L^{\frac{n-2}{2}}(S^n) such that the equation has no solution; this result is initially presented for half spheres with flat boundaries, specifically S^+_{n-1} = [0,π] × S^{n-2}, and key solutions involve blowing up at a single point with fixed index. Utilizing a finite energy solution framework developed in joint studies by the respective authors, this result can be applied to problems with boundaries that are compactly supported, yielding crucial insights for Nirenberg problem's solvability under challenging conditions where solutions may involve blowing up at infinity.

Deep learning models often rely on pre-defined, lower-dimensional feature representations to achieve success in both supervised and unsupervised settings. These models typically rely on the quality of these initial features, which can be poor without expert guidance. We propose a novel, unsupervised method that directly leverages high-dimensional data to directly learn improved feature representations, effectively bypassing the need for intermediate layers. Our approach builds on a set of unsupervised loss functions to develop a quality representation that achieves both cluster separation and diverse distribution coverage. The only external requirement of our technique is access to a 3D dataset, showcasing its potential in both 2D and 3D domains. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach in learning robust feature representations that surpass existing baselines.

Achieving significant contact tracing at scale is a major challenge for many countries during the COVID-19 pandemic. In the UK, a local model of collaboration between public health bodies and community groups is being used to implement contact tracing, but questions remain about its effectiveness and the impact of this approach on overall tracing yields. In this study, we developed a mathematical framework to simulate the potential effects of introducing a local tracing partnership on the ability of a national tracing scheme to identify and interrupt COVID-19 transmission in England. Our results indicate that by implementing a local tracing partnership, the national tracing system could miss approximately 25% more infections and 45% more transmissions, ultimately leading to an estimated 25% increase in undetected infections and 45% increase in transmissions. These findings could result in substantial disparities in COVID-19 transmission across different areas of the country.

Preliminary data from the Gaia mission, specifically Gaia DR2, were analyzed to determine the characteristics of the star cluster Melotte 72.  An initial investigation into the spatial distribution of the cluster revealed a significant deviation from uniformity, further supported by a binary system discovery within it, the presence of which was incorporated into future analyses.  Subsequently, the line-of-sight velocity of the cluster was calculated, yielding a velocity of 222.74 km/s, indicative of its membership in the field population and lack of association with the dwarf galaxy Leo I.  An age of 3.16 billion years was derived from the color-magnitude diagram, derived using binary systems as standards, and was further refined by employing a Bayesian analysis.  Utilizing a variety of theoretical models, the location of the cluster was determined to be at a distance of 12.4 kpc, and under the assumption of a uniform chemical composition, the uncertainty ranges were found to be 10.4 to 14.2 kpc.  An analysis of the cluster's morphology indicated no evidence of significant tidal distortion.

This study examines the distribution of Betti numbers in a topological model derived from a Gaussian random process, processed through a sparse random graph as it evolves over time in a progressive manner. We specifically investigate this system in the supercritical phase on a fixed scale and in the weak regime, focusing on the asymptotic behavior of the data as the system's size becomes very large. To achieve a comprehensive analysis, we develop novel methods for analyzing barycentric complexes generated by subgraphs of Poisson and Erdos-Renyi graphs, combining combinatorial analysis with probabilistic techniques. This in-depth analysis reveals that, under the supercritical phase, the average number of born simplex entities in a $k$-dimensional form is approximately equal to the expected number of such simplex entities, while those in the $k$ dimension are significantly less prevalent and their expected number is approximately equal to the $k$th expected value of such simplex entities. Furthermore, in the weak regime, we show that, with a very high degree of certainty, the average number of born simplex entities in a $k$ dimension is equal to the $k$th expected value of such simplex entities for all possible $k$ values. This significant result allows us to establish a more accurate understanding of the asymptotic distribution of data in the system.

This paper tackles the challenge of adjusting eye-in-hand cameras that exhibit vision errors due to manufacturing tolerances, a prevalent issue in robotics that goes unresolved by robotics learning approaches. A new unsupervised method is introduced that can be implemented using only one image and the camera's frame. The proposed solution involves a game-theory framework, where an agent optimizes camera calibration by assessing an image's quality through its own metric. A key innovation lies in the fact that this image quality metric is defined as the output of an image network, with the frame's coordinates also being the output, but trained in a different setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in simulating diverse sensor frames, and the results are validated by an eye-in-Hand CNN comparison. Furthermore, the Q-learn algorithm is found to be more suitable for this problem, and a fast convergence is observed after just one iteration.

In many cases, a pre-trained model's performance may be deemed inadequate to meet specific criteria set by domain experts. To address this issue, a groundbreaking approach known as Reverse Constrained Reinforcement Learning incorporates an inverse problem by optimizing a variable to achieve desired outcomes based on pre-existing policy information and goal descriptions. By framing the problem in an integrated framework, this paper explores both existence proofs and algorithms designed to solve this issue. An algorithm is presented with performance guarantees under specific assumptions, including heightened parameter sensitivity, and an example demonstrates that reverse problems can yield superior policies when parameterized correctly.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission is set to significantly advance our understanding of the Galaxy and its star populations by providing highly accurate astrometric and photometric data for over a billion stars, along with data for solar system objects. This breakthrough will be achieved through GAIA's exceptional precision in measuring stellar positions and parallaxes, as well as its comprehensive photometric coverage, spanning from UV to near-infrared wavelengths. Key areas of study that GAIA's data will support include determining stellar masses and ages, as well as investigating the Galaxy's structure, mass distribution, and mass-to-light ratio. Furthermore, GAIA's data will enable researchers to explore the Galaxy's evolution, its outer boundaries, and its mass loss over time. The study also addresses the unique capabilities of GAIA to detect and analyze stellar variability, chemical compositions, and dynamic phenomena such as planetary nebulae and pulsars. Finally, GAIA's data will provide valuable insights into the planet formation processes within the Solar System and the Galaxy.

For any graph with a treewidth $t$, we present two new linear-time, deterministic algorithms to create vertex partitions. Firstly, we show how to split a graph into two roughly equal subgraphs with a treewidth $O(t\log n)$. Secondly, we describe how to create subgraphs with treewidth $t$ by partitioning the graph into $k$ sets. Both algorithms require no more than a number $C$ of memory words, where $C$ is the number of vertices $n$. These results are achieved by combining memory-efficient graph operations with randomized techniques for tree decomposition, such as using a number $t$, and a depth $C$. This leads to a new understanding of the space complexity of deterministic tree decomposition. As a result, we have found a significant impact on the space efficiency of graph algorithms, allowing for a variety of applications to run with limited memory, such as finding a tree-like structure with a number $t$, or partitioning a graph into smaller components with a number $k$. Additionally, we have presented a new algorithm to represent cycles with a number $k$, using only a number $C$ memory words.

We examine the weighted grouping interpretation, commonly used to analyze the health of social and business networks, by incorporating directionality. This involves identifying communities within various networks, by maximizing a grouping quality metric based on weights and connections. The quality metric can be understood as the average number of links within each community, by normalizing weights and considering directionality. The quality metric is suitable for analyzing heterogeneous networks and can be mathematically maximized using methods like modularity and other optimization methods. The quality metric is shown to correlate strongly with human well-being and is also used as a measure of customer satisfaction in post-processing surveys. To maintain the validity of this measure, certain requirements for network data are established, based on observations from social science and marketing practices.

Physics-informed neural networks have emerged as a promising technique for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) in applied mathematics. By integrating PDE constraints into the loss function during training, these models can generalize to unseen equations. Nevertheless, their performance is heavily reliant on the choice of loss function and corresponding measurement points, making it difficult to determine their suitability for a given problem beforehand. This study proposes a post-hoc method for estimating errors in PI-NNs after training, offering guidance on where to implement boundary conditions, boundary, and initial conditions, and pinpointing regions that might need refined data collection. Our experiments validate the method's effectiveness for heat and advection-diffusion equations and pipe flow problems.

In this research, we examine the development of models to predict air contaminants in epidemiology studies, focusing on a novel framework combining geostatistics and the capabilities of machine learning. Our approach aims to address limitations in current models, which often rely heavily on location and time data, potentially overlooking essential individual characteristics. Additionally, a key challenge in the field is the difficulty in obtaining exposure assessments due to cost and privacy concerns. To overcome this limitation, we developed a flexible multivariate spatio-temporal model incorporating multiple sources of data, including private information from a reference dataset. Through simulation, we demonstrate that our approach yields accurate predictions and can effectively learn from private information without compromising individual privacy. Our proposed framework successfully integrates private data while preserving privacy.

Our research focuses on tunneling spectroscopy, specifically the interaction between a superconductor containing Majorana zero modes and an resistive superconductor. In the frequency range where the superconductor still retains its non-zero induced gap, the major vertex in the current operator is identified. By applying the tunneling spectroscopy technique, the relationship between the conductance and frequency can be determined. For an ohmic dissipative environment, the conductance exhibits a notable peak centered around the energy of Majorana zero modes. Notably, the shape and magnitude of this peak can reveal the coupling strength between the superconductor and the dissipative environment. Notably, the peak's characteristics can also reveal the dissipative environment's inductance. Our calculations show that a voltage bump can also occur at the Majorana zero mode energy level, with the conductance's response being influenced by the inductance value of the dissipative environment. Our research shows that the major vertex in the current operator has a broader range of applicability compared to Majorana-related processes found in other hybrid device types. Our research shows that the hybrid device using an ohmic dissipative environment can provide more distinct signals for Majorana zero modes compared to hybrid devices types.

We study a family of linear bandits with limited information, and notice that many dense estimation problems can be recast as this problem. Specifically, we consider a weighted permutation test for issues like A/B testing, Causal Inference with Noise, and Causal Inference without Noise, which are all subproblems in the bandit problem, and find it can be efficient in terms of time and sample complexity.

Graphene with energy gaps has a complex structure consisting of multiple sub-bands of Dirac cones connected by gaps, with each sub-band characterized by a distinct Berry phase. When a Zeeman gap is introduced through an external magnetic field, each sub-band develops a valley Hall effect that generates a current in response to a valley imbalance, with the current direction dependent on the valley index and electric field. Researchers have proposed that an alternative way to generate a valley Hall current is by applying an orbital anomalous Hall effect that arises from a non-uniform transverse electric field. This results in a valley Hall current in addition to the Chern insulating state in the case of a fully gapped graphone lattice.

The development of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has been a significant factor in solving Complex Graph Learning (CGL) problems successfully. GNNs learn from graph data using reinforcement learning and can adapt to changing environments, but GNNs based on reinforcement learning are vulnerable to data contamination due to the reliance on limited datasets for training. To address this, we introduce the concept of intentionally altering the training datasets to evaluate the resilience of GNNs in this specific context. Our approach involves analyzing how the contamination affects the performance of GNNs by employing alternative statistical distributions to replace the graphs in the training datasets. We present empirical findings on three prominent GNN methods across three well-known reinforcement learning tasks, demonstrating the impact of graph distribution on model performance and its counterintuitive nature compared to matrix-based deep learning methods.

The process of matching celestial objects across different surveys, which involves determining if objects in various catalogues represent the same entity, primarily depends on astrometric data. By integrating photometric information derived from objects' spectral energy distributions, we can enhance the matching process and thereby improve the quality of simulated data. Moreover, we can incorporate machine learning-based methods to leverage the spectral information in object photometric classification. Building upon the OGLE survey, we developed a photometric classification machine learning model trained on 11 distinct object types using real data from 152,542 objects, thereby achieving high accuracy. By incorporating these classifications and associated errors into the source code of the astrometric matching tool, MCMATCH, we observed that our approach significantly improves the matching performance by increasing correct matches and rejected non-match entries by 10-15%.

We present a minimal set of vertices, S, in an infinite graph G such that S can be embedded as a subset of G for every possible subgraph subG of G obtained by removing vertices. Additionally, for any possible subgraph subG of G, S remains embedded within subG. In general n-uniform graphs, this property holds unless there exists a particular subgraph subG of G, achieved by removing vertices, that contains an edge with missing vertices. In general n-uniform graphs, for every subG of G obtained by removing vertices and corresponding subgraph, S remains embedded within subG.Human-in-the-loop graph model training optimizes human and AI component contributions, enhancing performance over standard models while reducing annotation overhead and improving user experience.

The study focuses on a vertex subset S in an infinite graph G that can be embedded as a subset in every subgraph subG of G obtained by removing vertices. Additionally, S remains embedded within subG for any possible subG of G. In general n-uniform graphs, for every subG of G obtained by removing vertices, S remains embedded within subG. Furthermore, our analysis extends initially to hypergraphs. A study on uncountable graphs reveals additional properties related to minimal vertex sets for graph embedding.

Ontologies, crucial for knowledge representation in artificial intelligence, rely on graph visualization for easy comprehension. However, conventional visualization techniques fall short in depicting complex, real-world association patterns, particularly in large graphs with dense connections. OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation method developed to address these limitations, effectively showcases association patterns in large, densely connected data sets that are often overlooked in traditional visualization methods. Compared to standard visualization methods, OntoPlot effectively utilizes available space, significantly enhances readability, and accurately represents underlying association patterns.

This study introduces an innovative method to improve the performance of semi-supervised end-to-end (E2E) end-to-end automatic speech recognition. The proposed method involves using an unsupervised cycleGAN model to facilitate cross-domain speaker transformation without the need for a generator-discriminator pair, thereby enhancing the model's robustness to speaker variations. Experiment results on the Switchboard and Librispeech datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art method, with a significant improvement in the character error rate (11.7% to 11.4%).

This paper introduces an innovative approach to active navigation in mobile robots, which involves utilizing real-time image analysis to identify areas with potential obstacles. By leveraging a deep learning framework, we concentrate on predicting navigation paths and their associated uncertainty levels from raw images. Our system then incorporates an uncertainty calculation method to pinpoint areas of interest where paths are likely to deviate significantly. Consequently, our approach prioritizes collecting data from these areas to enhance the robustness of the predictor through a Bayesian model averaging method. Our proposed method achieves a notable improvement in 1) modeling accuracy as evidenced by quantitative evaluation and 2) efficiency in data collection, requiring updates in areas critical to navigation.

A key aspect of solving binary fluid mixture inversion issues is understanding the Soret effect in molecules with complex shapes. In this study, a theoretical model was developed to calculate the thermal diffusion factor for a mixture of monatomic and polyatomic fluids. Model outcomes showed that adding a rotational degree of freedom to molecules enhances their response to a thermal gradient, contributing significantly to thermal diffusion. Model predictions matched molecular dynamics simulations by incorporating dynamic interactions between the structural components of flexible molecules. Thicker molecules demonstrated increased sensitivity to the influence of their molecular shapes on thermal diffusion. Thorough analysis of our findings led to significant conclusions about how the thermodynamic properties of molecules with various shapes affect a mixture's thermal diffusion behavior.

Automated essay evaluation systems can provide cost-effective feedback in educational settings where professional grading is costly, such as when hundreds of students receive the same major feedback. Recent research has shown that using advanced transformer models for automated essay evaluation can yield better results than earlier methods, but these systems often come with high computational costs and significant latency. Our study proposes integrating ensemble techniques with efficient Pre-trained Position-wise Feed-Forward Networks (PWFFNs) to create a scalable and modular automated evaluation framework. By replacing the standard computational components in transformer models with more efficient counterparts and combining multiple models, we develop more reliable score predictions. Our framework involves training separate transformer models for each essay category, such as descriptive, narrative, and opinion pieces, and then using a weighted averaging method to determine the final evaluation score for a given input. Our framework, built using TwitEE, an optimized transformer model, demonstrates promising results on a range of benchmark datasets, showcasing its ability to deliver accurate scores and evaluations for automated essay assessment.

Deep learning-based object detectors have seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks to advancements in processing power and data availability. However, the advancement of domain adaptation techniques has been hindered by a lack of a domain shift specific evaluation metric and the reliance on supervised data for the target domain. In an effort to address these limitations, researchers have developed a novel domain adaptation strategy for pedestrian detection in autonomous vehicles. As vehicle driving behavior heavily relies on pedestrian actions, the pedestrian dataset has become a crucial resource. Unfortunately, the datasets collected from street scenes suffer from a domain gap when compared to the driving scene domain, leading to a high number of false positives. In order to address this issue, the researchers have proposed a new unsupervised technique called box re-ranking, which aims to reduce false positives by leveraging the information from unlabelled target domain data. The technique involves re-ordering detection boxes by considering the confidence scores of the models, the confidence of the color segmentation, and the confidence of the bounding box regression. In comparison to other domain adaptation methods, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art by a significant margin and also surpasses the combined effect of other top methods. The analysis reveals that the confidence score, the color segmentation, and the bounding box regression are all essential components for the successful implementation of the technique.

We introduce an innovative approach to elevate the quality of music recordings by combining two artificial intelligence techniques: artificial vocal synthesis and audio-based audio synthesis. Our method involves creating a universal audio-to-audio model for voices using a large dataset of high-quality audio material, followed by a specialized audio-to-audio model for individual voices based on limited material. To address the challenge of preserving musical context while transforming voices, we incorporate visual representation of audio, allowing for more informed audio synthesis. Our approach achieves high-quality audio synthesis for both general and personalized scenarios, demonstrating significant potential for applications in music streaming, audio post-production, and audio enhancement.

Our understanding of object dynamics is rooted in actions like throwing. To research how humans develop this skill, we need to examine the effect of one specific motion parameter, the point of release, on throwing performance. This study introduces a method to alter the release point during throwing motions. By superimposing a virtual force on the ball, we can delay its release and create a throwing motion where the release point differs from the agent's goal. This research finds that humans can adjust their aim in response to altered release points, even without direct feedback, and suggests that the release point is a critical factor in how humans plan and execute throwing motions.

Improving the performance of Neural Machine Translation with Syntax-based constraints is an ongoing pursuit for developing better language understanding. Recent advances in joint translation and parsing models have allowed for the creation of joint models that can learn valuable syntactic representations without relying on pre-trained models. However, these models typically only consider the translation score when outputting words during decoding. In contrast, we propose a new syntax-aware decoding strategy with dependencies, which allows for the joint output of words and parse tree during decoding. Our approach involves joint translation and syntax decoding in two separate stages. Experimental results conducted on two datasets, TED and WMT, demonstrate that our method surpasses previous state-of-the-art results, particularly on the TED dataset. Moreover, our output parse trees show greater correctness and better alignment with human annotations compared to traditional models.

A comprehensive distribution database, referred to as Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEP), has been created to gather and systematically compare quantum chemical binding energy data that's crucial for astrochemistry. We initially focused on the binary complexes involving water and carbon monoxide, which are significant in astrochemistry, and computed their binding energies with various cluster sizes and arrangements in the gas phase. This was done using two levels of density functional theory. Notably, the DFT method showed significant dispersion in its results, underestimating and overestimating the BEP reference values by up to 1.5 kJ/mol. This inconsistency underscores the necessity for further development in how DFT functionals account for dispersion. By categorizing the complexes according to their binding characteristics, we can make educated guesses about the behavior of similar molecules not yet included in the database. This information is vital for astrochemists, particularly when evaluating the validity of spectral features in ice mixtures and understanding the dynamics of these systems during ice formation.

Models that multiply random variables over time are common in many fields, such as economics, finance, and health, to assess cumulative effects. We studied a specific statistical model, providing estimates and testing the accuracy of the estimates. The model assumes a process where each step multiplies the previous value, preventing it from going below a specific threshold that depends on the available data, such as previous estimates. The lower threshold ensures the estimates remain realistic and doesn't significantly affect the model's performance. The model's performance is comparable to the standard model that doesn't have a lower threshold. The standard model has the property of being consistently accurate and providing reliable estimates as more data becomes available, supporting this performance. The typical accuracy of the estimates can be estimated using a straightforward approach. The typical accuracy is influenced by the number of data points and the initial values but can be further improved with a specific threshold that doesn't significantly affect the estimates. The typical accuracy converges to the performance of the standard model as more data becomes available.

This study presents an approach for measuring quantum states without requiring full quantum tomography. Specifically, we aim to calculate the purity of individual quantum state components and their expected value by using shallow measurements on a smaller subset of the quantum state. This method outperforms other approaches, such as randomized shadow Hamiltonian estimation, in terms of the precision of the estimates. We believe that our technique will facilitate high-precision benchmarking of quantum algorithms and error correction methods.

The reflection coefficient's $|k|$ behavior for the Davey-Stewartson II equations is analyzed and characterized through direct Riemann-Hilbert problem methods, providing significant insights into the asymptotic behavior of the non-linear solution as $x$ grows. These findings are corroborated by numerical methods, showcasing the relevance for both DS-II-I and DS-II-II types, with the latter exhibiting a phase shift at the reflection phase.

This paper focuses on text classification using a modified game-theoretic framework. Traditional game-theoretic classification, such as the Sybilit algorithm, is effective at increasing recommended item diversity but lacks robustness in handling malicious users. To address this limitation, we propose the Robust Sibylvariant (RSV) algorithm, a novel game-theoretic approach designed to maintain player diversity even in the presence of malicious users. The RSV algorithm's parameters are optimized via the Nonlinear Constrained Optimization (NCO) method, allowing it to adapt to varying user conditions and ensure robust performance. Our results, obtained through a comparison with various baseline and state-of-the-art algorithms, confirm the RSV algorithm's effectiveness. Notably, when employed as a filtering layer for Sybil-resistant algorithms like Fast-Sibyl, the RSV algorithm delivers enhanced performance.

A key goal in learning meta-strategies for adaptation is to learn a meta-representation of tasks in a way that supports meta-learning outcomes. However, it is often unclear whether the meta-representations being trained actually facilitate adaptation or not. In this work, we propose a key innovation: using data augmentation in meta-learning tasks, which we believe can confirm the quality of a meta-representation in terms of its adaptability. Our approach focuses on linear representations as they are widely used in meta-learning. We first establish a theory on linear representations, outlining their essential properties and how to quantify these properties. Based on this foundation, we then establish a set of linear representation properties that guarantee adaptability. We demonstrate that the theoretical results define the boundaries of effective meta-strategies in linear representation learning. We also show that the considered properties lead to effective learning approaches, and experimental results validate the theory's validity and provide insights into what makes a meta-representation successful.

In the past, researchers have utilized knowledge distillation to create smaller multilingual translation models. This technique involves training a smaller yet effective model from a more powerful one. However, a critical question remains unresolved: can this smaller model, achieved through distillation, maintain its performance when the model is modified in various ways. Our study, focusing on English to eight less-resourced language translations, investigates the different phases of distillation to identify which approaches lead to the most effective smaller models. Our key finding shows that smaller models developed in the final stages of distillation are more consistently successful. This research also examines how the choice of pre-trained multilingual models impacts the distillation process. Ultimately, our work contributes to the development of efficient smaller multilingual translation models.

We introduce an original theory in Minkowski space, featuring a hypergraph's Lagrangian density. We analyze the mock theoretical results through a step-by-step derivation. By incorporating genuine observations into a theoretical framework, the process of gaining knowledge occurs - although the theory under consideration is a fake one, as it involves no real physical properties.

The identification of pneumonia in CT scans is becoming increasingly crucial, especially with the growth of healthcare service digitalization. To address this challenge, researchers have been focusing on developing computer-aided diagnosis systems. The difficulty in creating these systems lies in training deep learning models, especially when dealing with a large amount of data. To overcome this limitation, this paper presents an innovative method involving extensive data enhancement techniques designed to reduce the need for extensive labelled data. By applying these techniques to a kidney dataset, this study demonstrates that a significant reduction in training error is achieved, accompanied by improved accuracy in detecting pneumonia regions. Moreover, by breaking down the data enhancement process into distinct stages, this study enables the efficient evaluation of each technique and identifies the most effective strategies for improving performance. To verify the effectiveness of this method, a comparison is conducted against a basic convolutional neural network with and without data enhancement, resulting in promising outcomes that highlight the efficacy of the proposed technique.

An image's content can be described by text, but a single description often falls short of conveying the full scope of an image. To address this limitation, we've developed a method for creating adjustable image descriptions through prompting. A prompt consists of a template with fillable details, such as "A [subject] [action] in a [setting]". Given an image and a prompt template, we've developed a new approach that's different from traditional models. This new approach consists of two key components: a prompt vector generator that creates the fundamental structure, and an adaptive subject feature extractor that incorporates both shared and individual characteristics of image content into the prompt vector. Additionally, we've used a training example re-weighting strategy to ensure accurate control over generated descriptions. To assess the quality of generated descriptions, we've developed a flexible evaluation metric, allowing for the identification of various types of errors. Our experimental results demonstrate that this new approach achieves a higher level of accuracy and precision than traditional image description models.

A fundamental aspect of common sense, causation and accountability in AI systems, is the concept of harm. Despite this, current artificial intelligence models for natural language understanding are inadequate in addressing it. This paper aims to investigate the definition of harm, exploring its key components, underlying causation, and moral implications. By analyzing a dataset of scenarios, we aim to develop a more nuanced model of harm that considers not just the outcome but also the intent behind actions. Our findings reveal that current AI language models struggle to distinguish between different types of harm, likely due to their limitation in capturing the complexity of moral reasoning. Ultimately, we propose a more refined model of harm that can serve as a foundation for moral and legal reasoning in artificial intelligence systems.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an open-source Big Learning framework that integrates Spark and sparklyr, a deep learning package within R, to facilitate various task-agnostic machine learning and deep learning operations on big data distributed systems. The inherent flexibility of Big Learning, allows for seamless adaptation to new optimization techniques and architectural innovations for deep learning. The MMLSpark package supports numerous popular deep learning networks and architectures and provides functionality for standard machine learning procedures such as parameter tuning, cross-validation, and hyperparameter optimization. The demonstration involves evaluating the performance of standard and graph convolutional networks on the CIFAR-10 and CelebA datasets, with the latter being trained on a massive scale comprising over 200,000 images utilizing a 16-node cluster.

Voice synthesis is typically achieved through a two-step process: 
first, text is converted to a form representing an average voice called 
intermediate representations and then this is combined with a chosen voice 
to generate speech. Our study introduces a novel method, Zero-shot Voice 
Conversion and Transformation, which can convert an unrecorded language into 
another while preserving that language's characteristics. Our approach uses 
intermediate representations and classifies languages based on their 
features in the intermediate space. Our results show that training language 
pair models can accurately classify unfamiliar languages. Our model can also 
synthesize speeches that align with unexplored languages, resulting in a 
significant improvement of 13-33% in accuracy. Our approach was implemented 
using a text-to-speech system. Our findings suggest an alternative 
approach for creating speech synthesis systems that can replicate particular 
speakers' voices and translate their language.

This investigation focuses on thermally consistent models described by generalized Fourier-Coleman-Gurtin and heat equations, applicable to a single component system under specific conditions. These models incorporate novel physical phenomena that take into account the anisotropic nature of material properties on a microscopic scale. Through the use of a Lagrange multiplier method, we develop and solve a system of equations representing the evolution of thermal conductivity and internal variable temperature. To ensure the solution's stability and reliability, we also establish key findings, including the maximum principle, the non-negative nature of the boundary flux, and the convergence of the boundary values as the boundary conditions evolve.

The widespread adoption of smart meters enables a precise understanding of the behavior of individual consumers. This vast amount of data can be harnessed to provide the low voltage grid operator with more accurate insights and better energy management in real-time and day-to-day operations. Focusing on the French low voltage grid, our study aims to develop a forecasting system for the daily 15-minute energy consumption profiles. This system combines multiple short-term load predictions with historical data and peak daily forecasts. The results show that on average, the forecasting accuracy can achieve a mean absolute percentage error of 4.5% for short-term and 6.6% for day-ahead predictions.

The increasing popularity of AI-driven problem solving in the context of machine learning has led to significant advancements. However, the effectiveness of these advancements can be compromised by the substantial costs associated with data collection and the challenges associated with data scarcity. To mitigate these issues, domain knowledge integration has become a crucial strategy for enhancing problem-solving capabilities and reducing the dependence on large datasets. This report aims to provide a comprehensive overview of methods for incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning models, thereby enabling the development of more accurate algorithms even when data is scarce.

In recent years, deep neural networks have significantly improved performance on a variety of image classification tasks in computer vision applications, particularly in medical imaging. Despite this, their reliance on large amounts of meticulously labeled data, coupled with potential biases, has hindered their ability to be deployed effectively in real-world medical settings. The increasing severity of the COVID-19 pandemic has created an urgent need for effective and diverse detection, diagnosis, and segmentation tools for lung abnormalities on CT scans, necessitating models that can work effectively even with limited labeling.

Our research proposes an innovative approach to accurately identify and isolate lung pathologies in CT scans using minimal labeling and simple image-level annotations. This involves training two convolutional neural networks, one capable of accurate multi-class classification, and another focused on precise localization of lesions. The model's experimental evaluation demonstrates competitive performance compared to current state-of-the-art models, while significantly reducing the need for extensive labeling and annotation.

Furthermore, we have extensively analyzed the potential bias in our models by employing an unbiased assessment framework using sub-sampling techniques. Our results indicate that the proposed model is largely immune to bias when using an unbiased assessment framework, and when employing data augmentation, it can achieve a mean unbiased mIoU score close to that of the mean IoU score for the Lung Nodule Detection dataset.

Recent research utilizing deep learning has significantly advanced the accuracy of automated vertebra localization and identification from computed tomography (CT) scans, but this progress is frequently hindered by limitations in the training data and computational resources. For instance, top-performing approaches often rely on vast datasets comprising thousands of images prepared through tedious manual segmentation, which hinders the development of cutting-edge technology. Moreover, these methods require complex and time-consuming scanning procedures, which often yield suboptimal results. Therefore, there is a pressing need for simplified and more efficient solutions that can be trained with minimal data and produce reliable outcomes without compromising performance. In this study, a novel, automated vertebra localization and identification system is introduced that features superior performance in comparison to current state-of-the-art methods, while solely learning from a compact dataset of 30 carefully designed synthetic scans. By combining synthetic and real-world data, the proposed rectification and optimization strategy successfully simplifies the complexity of vertebra localization and identification by 40% and 80% respectively, and boasts the remarkable ability to be trained with a mere 10 training samples, and still yield impressive accuracy rates of 91.3% and 80.7% respectively, and the capability to detect and identify 99.1% of vertebrae in test scans. The innovative system achieves its remarkable results with a remarkably low computational requirement, and the source code is publicly available.

Our study demonstrates that the strong interaction between light and matter can stabilize an unstable electron scenario over multiple scattering cycles by means of an isolated, unstable state, which is consistently represented within the system's Hamiltonian. This conclusion is reached through a theoretical model that combines real-time quantum dynamics of electrons in metals with the quantum theory of optical light-matter interactions, and is validated experimentally through the correlation of electron and light dynamics in real-time. Specifically, the light's interaction with the metal causes it to emit scattered photons in an ultrafast pulse with a duration that far exceeds its arrival time. As a result, the vacuum fluctuations' effect on electrons within the metal leads to a significant slowdown in the speed of the emitted light pulse by over one order of magnitude.

In the field of legged robots, selecting the optimal actuator stiffness is crucial for achieving stable locomotion. Currently, most research focuses on designing specialized actuators or utilizing pre-determined joint angle profiles, both of which are limited in adaptability and effectiveness across diverse terrains. To address this issue, we introduce a novel machine learning approach that utilizes simulated Quadrupedbots equipped with elastic actuators, enabling the direct optimization of joint stiffness settings as part of the locomotion policy. This results in the development of a simulated Quadrupedbot capable of navigating diverse terrains with improved stability and efficiency compared to fully actuated counterparts. Moreover, we extend our approach to a physical Quadrupedbot by treating the hyperparameters of the simulated model as adjustable joint angle offsets, thereby achieving comparable performance on diverse natural terrain segments.

We propose a novel variational approach, centered around a functional that quantifies the distance between arbitrary quantum states and the set of separable states. This core functional serves as an upper bound for the entanglement measure of any given state. Moreover, its value becomes zero for purely classical probability distributions over product states. Our method offers an efficient means to approximate the separability set, facilitating the assessment of states for practical applications, such as quantum image recognition.

A small-scale tearing instability has been discovered in collisionless magnetic slabs with a uniform background magnetic field. The instability arises due to the interaction between Alfvénic shear flow and collisional effects, which dominate the small-scale regime. Analytical research reveals that the growth rate of this small-scale tearing mode depends on the Alfvén speed, collisionality, compressibility, and Alfvénic shear flow characteristics. The mode has key properties distinguishing it from its large-scale counterpart: it has growth rates proportional to collisionality, complex komponent behavior, and can create highly resistive islands. Simulations confirm these findings and demonstrate that the small-scale growth rate is insensitive to magnetic field configuration but depends on flow profile. The results suggest that the microscale tearing instability can contribute to magnetic reconnection and electron acceleration in collisionless environments, particularly when electron temperature gradients are involved.

The concept of intrinsic properties has gained popularity in e-commerce due to its capacity to enhance user engagement and boost product visibility. Nonetheless, the standard approach of employing image features derived from a query image falls short as users typically prefer to browse properties associated with identity features. We propose a technique to shift query images into desired feature domains using generative adversarial networks and propose semi-supervised learning for efficient utilization of limited labeled training data and preservation of target feature attributes. We also introduce performance evaluation via ranking images based on relevance scores for fashion image retrieval through features. Through synthesis of fashion images with inherent properties, our approach facilitates users in browsing relevant items associated with properties associated with desired characteristics.

In certain nonlinear inverse problems, such as solving equations $Ax = f$ in a generalized framework, employing a traditional Tikhonov regularization approach often results in overly complex and computationally intensive solutions to a potentially unnecessary degree. A more streamlined and efficient alternative, the dual gradient method, is proposed as a solution. This innovative approach is based on the dual problem formulation, where the method converges at the same rate as the more widely used dual Tikhonov regularization, yet leverages the simplicity and efficiency of gradient-based optimization techniques. A comprehensive proof of its convergence for both dual metrics and norms is provided, along with assumptions under which these forms of convergence are achievable.

Research into light field depth estimation has been gaining momentum in recent years, primarily because low-resolution boundary images can't provide sufficient details for accurate depth estimation, where the sparsity of rays per sub-aperture becomes a challenge, particularly in areas where objects are occluded or nearly so. To address this issue, we suggest incorporating an additional channel in the depth estimation network that produces a cost map, specifically tailored for occluded areas. Our experiments using the HDFD benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in overall depth estimation performance.

The inverse scattering method's bilinear technique for the Fokas-Lenells equations was the focus of a recent study, where researchers derived the necessary equations and potential functions for the method and used the gauge transformation to broaden the approach to nonlinear equations.

Our study focuses specifically on the double torsion component of the double field theory action, exploring its implications in a non-Riemannian context. By analyzing the double torsion sector more closely, we derive an expression that resembles the Kruskal action under specific conditions where the sole non-zero structure group element is two, i.e., B=1. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of the doubled curvature tensor stemming from this action, providing the corresponding equation that results when B=2. Our findings also yield insights into the relationship between the non-Riemannian sector of the DFT action and the nonmetricity associated with a generalization of Weyl gravity that incorporates a skew-symmetric 2-form potential.

In indoor WiFi settings, end users frequently encounter coverage gaps that necessitate wireless extender installations.  However, excessive reliance on extenders can degrade overall network performance.  To resolve these issues, the IEEE 802.11 Working Group has developed technologies such as Multi-AP Coordination and Trigger-Based Multi-AP Coordination, which optimize performance in networks comprising multiple Access Points (APs) and Extenders (EXTs).  Despite these advancements, EXT owners often lack vital information required to establish proper coordination, given their limited technical expertise.  Consequently, the goal of this research is to assist EXT owners in selecting appropriate coordination methods by evaluating the load on the associated AP.  To achieve this, we have devised a system capable of identifying when an EXT owner should switch to a different AP by leveraging real-time monitoring and data enabled through IEEE 802.11k and 802.11v protocols.  To systematize this process, we have developed a set of heuristics and evaluated their effectiveness through simulations and live trials, demonstrating a significant improvement in network throughput and reduced latency when transitioning to less loaded networks.
